content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.8. I used 46 of the 60 budget.

The deciding factor was whether a task cost little because its rules had been trained before, or because its input-output mapping looked like a trained task. Cost followed whether the rules were already trained. Similarity barely mattered.

| Condition | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|
| All rules new, before training (L1-S1-M1, L1-S3-M4) | ~33 (n=4) |
| L4-S4-M4: all rules new, but fairly similar to trained tasks (max overlap 0.56) | ~44 (n=3) |
| L1-S1-M1: each rule trained twice, low similarity (max 0.375) | ~19 (n=10) |
| L4-S3-M2: two of its rules trained only once, low similarity (0.375) | ~22 (n=9) |
| L4-S4-M2: every rule trained only once, low similarity (0.375) | ~19 (n=8) |

- **Holistic is unlikely.** L4-S4-M4 was more similar to the trained tasks than L1-S1-M1, yet it cost about twice as much, because its rules were new.
- **Factor-when-justified (k=2 or 3) is unlikely.** It only reuses a rule after seeing it in 2 or 3 trained tasks. L4-S4-M2's rules had each been seen once and it had low similarity, so this learner should have found it nearly as hard as a brand-new task. It was as cheap as L1-S1-M1. One exposure to a rule was enough for reuse, which is the part-based pattern.

**Caveats:**
- The noise is heavy-tailed: the same test returned anything from 1 to 44.
- The comparison against similarity rests on only 3 samples of L4-S4-M4. That's why the confidence isn't higher.
- One result fits part-based less well. L1-S3-M4 has one new rule, so it should have cost more than the zero-new-rule tasks. It came out about the same (~17, n=5), which is within the noise.
